- **self**: Supplements: CoQ10, creatine, vitamin D, Mucuna and failed neuroprotectants (14/3)

## Measurements and reference values

- [statement] In the NINDS NET-PD program, a randomized phase II futility trial of creatine and minocycline (Neurology 2006) found that neither could be rejected as futile and recommended considering both for definitive phase III trials, whereas the later Long-term Study 1 of creatine monohydrate 10 g/d (JAMA 2015; 1741 participants) was terminated early for futility at a planned interim analysis (n = 955) and concluded that creatine did not improve clinical outcomes. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16481597/ · keywords: Supplements: CoQ10, creatine, vitamin D, Mucuna and failed neuroprotectants · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4349346/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13442935/
- [statement] Two analyses of commercial Mucuna pruriens products reported wide variation in levodopa content: a 2018 HPLC analysis of six products found levodopa content varying from 6% to 141% of label claims with no product within the 90%–110% pharmacopeial limits, and a 2022 JAMA Neurology case series of 16 analyzed supplements found 15 containing levodopa at 2 mg to 241 mg per recommended serving, with actual levodopa 228% to 2186% greater than the estimate for products listing a seed-extract quantity, while carbidopa and benserazide were not detected. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5808387/ · keywords: Supplements: CoQ10, creatine, vitamin D, Mucuna and failed neuroprotectants · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9361182/

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] Two coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) trials in early Parkinson disease reported conflicting results: an eighty-subject dosage-ranging trial (Arch Neurol 2002) reported less functional decline at 1200 mg/d than with placebo (P =.04) and concluded that CoQ10 appears to slow deterioration pending confirmation in a larger study, while the phase III QE3 trial (600 participants; JAMA Neurol 2014) was terminated after a prespecified futility criterion was reached and showed no evidence of clinical benefit; a 2026 review suggests the discrepancies might stem from different sample sizes and study durations. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12374491/ · keywords: Supplements: CoQ10, creatine, vitamin D, Mucuna and failed neuroprotectants · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24664227/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13442935/
- [statement] Two published meta-analyses of randomized trials of coenzyme Q10 in Parkinson disease reported no significant benefit over placebo: a 2016 analysis of five RCTs (981 patients) found that the overall effect did not favor either group for total UPDRS, and a 2017 analysis of eight studies (899 patients) found a pooled WMD of 1.02 for UPDRS part 3 (p = 0.54) and stated that routine CoQ10 treatment of PD could not be recommended. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26553164/ · keywords: Supplements: CoQ10, creatine, vitamin D, Mucuna and failed neuroprotectants · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27830343/
- [statement] A 2014 Cochrane review (searches to 10 November 2013; two RCTs, 194 patients) reported no clear evidence of an effect of creatine on motor function (MD -0.26; 95% CI -4.39 to 3.88; low quality evidence) and judged the evidence base limited by risk of bias, small sample sizes and short duration, and a 2017 BMC Neurology meta-analysis (five RCTs, 1339 participants) reported no significant differences in total, mental, activities of daily living or motor UPDRS scores, with an improvement in Schwab & England Scale scores, and concluded that creatine has no observed benefit in PD. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10196714/ · keywords: Supplements: CoQ10, creatine, vitamin D, Mucuna and failed neuroprotectants · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5457735/
- [statement] Published conclusions on isradipine in early Parkinson disease differ: the STEADY-PD III trial (336 patients; 5 mg of immediate-release isradipine twice daily or placebo for 36 months) reported that long-term treatment did not slow clinical progression (treatment effect -0.27 point, P = 0.85), whereas a re-analysis of STEADY-PD II data (10 mg/day extended-release isradipine) reported significantly smaller UPDRS scores than placebo at the end of the 52-week trial, with post hoc adjustment for symptomatic therapy diminishing the statistical significance, and suggested that clinically attainable brain exposure to isradipine may slow early-stage progression. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7465126/ · keywords: Supplements: CoQ10, creatine, vitamin D, Mucuna and failed neuroprotectants · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8922308/
- [statement] In a randomized trial of tocopherol (a component of vitamin E) and deprenyl in early Parkinson's disease (800 patients assigned to placebo, tocopherol, deprenyl or both; N Engl J Med 1993), there was no beneficial effect of tocopherol or any interaction between tocopherol and deprenyl, and a 2026 review likewise reports that no benefits of vitamin E were seen in UPDRS total score. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8417384/ · keywords: Supplements: CoQ10, creatine, vitamin D, Mucuna and failed neuroprotectants · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13442935/
- [statement] Reports on vitamin D supplementation and motor outcomes in Parkinson disease are mixed: a double-blind placebo-controlled trial (114 patients; vitamin D3 1200 IU/d for 12 months; Am J Clin Nutr 2013) reported that vitamin D3 significantly prevented deterioration of the Hoehn and Yahr stage (P = 0.005), a 2025 meta-analysis of 8 randomized trials (646 cases) found no reduction in UPDRS part III but a benefit on 6-Minute walking test distance, and a 2026 randomized trial (2000 IU/d for 12 weeks) reported no significant improvement in motor function; a 2026 review judged that firm conclusions on the disease-modifying potential of vitamin D cannot yet be drawn. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23485413/ · keywords: Supplements: CoQ10, creatine, vitamin D, Mucuna and failed neuroprotectants · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12183021/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13406316/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13442935/
- [statement] NICE guideline NG71 (published 19 July 2017), section 1.6 on pharmacological neuroprotective therapy, recommends against using vitamin E as a neuroprotective therapy for people with Parkinson's disease (1.6.1) and against using co-enzyme Q10 as a neuroprotective therapy except in the context of clinical trials (1.6.2), both marked as 2006, amended 2017; a 2026 review reports that CoQ10 is classified as non-efficacious for delaying progression of PD by both the International Parkinson & Movement Disorders Society and the National Institute for Health Care Excellence at the time of writing. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/Recommendations · keywords: Supplements: CoQ10, creatine, vitamin D, Mucuna and failed neuroprotectants · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13442935/
- [statement] NICE guideline NG71 (published 19 July 2017) recommends in 1.7.13 that people with Parkinson's disease be advised to take a vitamin D supplement, in 1.7.14 that creatine supplements not be offered to people with Parkinson's disease, and in 1.7.15 that people with Parkinson's disease be advised not to take over-the-counter dietary supplements without first consulting their pharmacist or other healthcare professional; a 2026 review distinguishes supplements used to correct deficiencies, such as vitamin D for bone health, which it places outside its scope, from supplements explored for disease-modifying potential. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/Recommendations · keywords: Supplements: CoQ10, creatine, vitamin D, Mucuna and failed neuroprotectants · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13442935/
- [statement] The American Academy of Neurology practice parameter on neuroprotective strategies and alternative therapies for Parkinson disease (Neurology 2006) reported the conclusions that no treatment has been shown to be neuroprotective and that there is no evidence that vitamin or food additives can improve motor function in PD; a 2026 review states that multiple phase II and III trials of pharmacological agents aimed at modulating PD pathophysiological hallmarks all failed to demonstrate significant disease-modifying effects. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16606908/ · keywords: Supplements: CoQ10, creatine, vitamin D, Mucuna and failed neuroprotectants · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13442935/

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] In the SURE-PD3 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (298 participants with early PD at 58 US sites; inosine titrated to raise serum urate to 7.1-8.0 mg/dL, n = 149, versus placebo, n = 149, for up to 2 years), the study closed early after a prespecified interim futility analysis and MDS-UPDRS progression rates did not differ significantly (11.1 points per year for inosine versus 9.9 for placebo; difference 1.26, 95% CI -0.59 to 3.11; P = .18); more kidney stones occurred with inosine (7.0 versus 1.4 stones per 100 patient-years) and the authors concluded the findings do not support inosine as a treatment for early PD. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8441591/ · keywords: Supplements: CoQ10, creatine, vitamin D, Mucuna and failed neuroprotectants · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13442935/
- [statement] In a double-blind, randomized, controlled, crossover study (Neurology 2017) of single-dose intake in eighteen patients with advanced Parkinson disease, Mucuna pruriens (MP) powder from roasted seeds at a high dose containing 17.5 mg/kg of levodopa induced greater motor improvement at 90 and 180 minutes, longer ON duration and fewer dyskinesias than dispersible levodopa plus benserazide (3.5 mg/kg), and the authors concluded that single-dose MP met all noninferiority efficacy and safety outcome measures; a 2025 systematic review likewise states that this trial found MP significantly reduced dyskinesia at both 90 and 180 min compared to levodopa plus a decarboxylase inhibitor. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5539737/ · keywords: Supplements: CoQ10, creatine, vitamin D, Mucuna and failed neuroprotectants · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12377966/
- [statement] Sources differ on adverse events with Mucuna pruriens (MP) in Parkinson disease: a 2025 systematic review (5 clinical trials, 108 participants; one study rated high quality, one with some concerns and three low quality) found MP associated with fewer adverse events and no dyskinesia reported while calling current clinical evidence limited, whereas a 12-month open-label phase 2 randomized trial in thirty-two untreated patients reported more frequent adverse events with MP than with levodopa plus a decarboxylase inhibitor (56% vs. 37.5%, p = 0.48; not statistically significant) and stated that larger double-blind trials with extended follow-up of 24–36 months are needed. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12377966/ · keywords: Supplements: CoQ10, creatine, vitamin D, Mucuna and failed neuroprotectants · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13347555/

## Research summary — Supplements: CoQ10, creatine, vitamin D, Mucuna and failed neuroprotectants

Trial evidence for supplements and failed neuroprotectants in Parkinson disease is largely negative in the sources read. Large trials of coenzyme Q10 (QE3), creatine (NET-PD LS-1), inosine (SURE-PD3) and isradipine (STEADY-PD III) each reported no clinical benefit, as did a tocopherol trial. Earlier signals, a CoQ10 dosage-ranging trial reporting a positive trend and a creatine futility screen that did not reject it, were followed by later large trials reporting no benefit. Vitamin D reports are mixed. Mucuna pruriens trials are small and short, and commercial products varied widely from labelled levodopa. NICE NG71 recommends against vitamin E and, except in the context of clinical trials, against co-enzyme Q10 as neuroprotective therapy, recommends that creatine supplements not be offered, and advises a vitamin D supplement. This summarizes what sources report; it is not medical advice.

## Source disagreement — Supplements: CoQ10, creatine, vitamin D, Mucuna and failed neuroprotectants

A 2002 CoQ10 dosage-ranging trial reported a significant 1200-mg/d versus placebo difference (P =.04) and concluded CoQ10 appears to slow functional decline, while the 2014 QE3 phase III trial reported no evidence of clinical benefit.

## Open question — Supplements: CoQ10, creatine, vitamin D, Mucuna and failed neuroprotectants

Whether NICE NG71 recommendations 1.6.1, 1.6.2, 1.7.13, 1.7.14 and 1.7.15 changed after the 19 July 2017 publication date was not established; the pinned page shows no later update date.
